steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computational linguistics paper presenting the 2023 version of the Spanish Resource Grammar. Explain why formal implemented grammars still matter for NLP, what is new in this version and why reviving the grammar is worthwhile, and end with an outline of the paper.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Among the different approaches to computational linguistics, formal grammars are a link between linguistic theory and natural language processing (NLP). By formal grammars we mean linguistic formalisms that are fully explicit and that encode the general principles and operations involved in generating syntactic structure. These formalisms are tied to fully-fledged theories of syntax and linguists develop them independently of specific NLP needs or tasks. For example, Minimalism, Lexical Functional Grammar and Head-driven Phrase Structure Grammar are linguistic theories of syntax. On the other hand, the Penn-Treebank (PTB) and the Universal Dependencies do not explicitly encode why something should get a certain label, so we consider them labeling conventions and not fully-fledged theories of syntax. It is hard to make sure that a labeling convention for complex structure is followed consistently. Formal grammars, in contrast, encode complex linguistic hypotheses explicitly, and also, when they are implemented on the computer, they map sentences to structures automatically and they are fully consistent. Any error in them can be fixed in a systematic way. Then any data that was labeled before can be re-labeled automatically.

Grammars take a long time to develop, and the structures they produce are harder to use than the annotation schemes developed specifically for NLP. For example, parsing can be a lot slower and the software stack usually has to be more complex. But grammars are still one of the few clear and long-term links between linguistics and NLP. In recent practice, formal implemented grammars have been used for computer assisted language learning (CALL) applications, including grammar coaching. They have also been used to create high quality treebanks for training semantic parsers. In particular, one of these studies reports a 35% error reduction and 14% absolute accuracy gain because they used the precise and consistent semantic representations generated by the English Resource Grammar. In this paper we present the latest version of a grammar that can be used to create this kind of high quality training data for Spanish.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Among the different approaches to computational linguistics, formal grammars are a link between linguistic theory and natural language processing (NLP). By formal grammars we mean linguistic formalisms that are fully explicit and that encode the general principles and operations involved in generating syntactic structure. These formalisms are tied to fully-fledged theories of syntax and linguists develop them independently of specific NLP needs or tasks. For example, Minimalism, Lexical Functional Grammar and Head-driven Phrase Structure Grammar are linguistic theories of syntax. On the other hand, the Penn-Treebank (PTB) and the Universal Dependencies do not explicitly encode why something should get a certain label, so we consider them labeling conventions and not fully-fledged theories of syntax. It is hard to make sure that a labeling convention for complex structure is followed consistently. Formal grammars, in contrast, encode complex linguistic hypotheses explicitly, and also, when they are implemented on the computer, they map sentences to structures automatically and they are fully consistent. Any error in them can be fixed in a systematic way. Then any data that was labeled before can be re-labeled automatically.

Grammars take a long time to develop, and the structures they produce are harder to use than the annotation schemes developed specifically for NLP. For example, parsing can be a lot slower and the software stack usually has to be more complex. But grammars are still one of the few clear and long-term links between linguistics and NLP. In recent practice, formal implemented grammars have been used for computer assisted language learning (CALL) applications, including grammar coaching. They have also been used to create high quality treebanks for training semantic parsers. In particular, one of these studies reports a 35% error reduction and 14% absolute accuracy gain because they used the precise and consistent semantic representations generated by the English Resource Grammar. In this paper we present the latest version of a grammar that can be used to create this kind of high quality training data for Spanish.

The Spanish Resource Grammar is the second biggest implemented HPSG grammar (see § 2.1). The latest version, which we present here, uses a newer morphophonological analyzer through a Python interface that is completely reimplemented and easy to edit. With the new interface the grammar can be used with the state-of-the-art HPSG parsers and tailored as necessary. We report the accuracy of the SRG on a portion of the AnCora/TIBIDABO corpus for the first time, and we present an example of using a learner corpus to find areas where the grammar's encoded analyses can be improved.

The work we present is unusual because we are breathing new life into a valuable resource that was dormant for at least 10 years. Grammars, unlike other software, do not become obsolete, in the sense that they encode robust linguistic theories. That is why we are convinced that the SRG should be reintegrated into the computational linguistics landscape, so the community has a resource similar to the English Resource Grammar (ERG). But like other software, grammars do become obsolete because they depend on tools that can become outdated, and fixing these dependencies can be expensive. We present a year of work that went into making the SRG work with a better parser and establishing its accuracy on 2K sentences. This is a time consuming process, but it only has to be done once, and then automatic tools can be used to quickly compare new iterations. On this foundation the grammar can be expanded so that its coverage improves.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we briefly explain the formalism behind the grammar implementation and what treebanking means in grammar engineering. We also have a section crediting the original version of the grammar, which took its author years to build. Section 3 describes what we did to bring the SRG up to date with the SOTA grammar engineering tools. Section 4 is about evaluation. It gives an overview of a set of phenomena that are covered, as shown by a specially constructed test suite (§ 4.1); it presents the results of parsing 2,291 sentences from a Spanish news corpus with the grammar (§ 4.2), and discusses the issues that the evaluation shows; and the results for 100 sentences from a Spanish learner corpus (§ 4.3). Section 4.3 has an example of how the implemented grammar helps to study syntactic hypotheses rigorously. The example shows a tension in the analyses that would probably be overlooked if one did not implement them on the computer and did not run the grammar on a corpus with ungrammatical examples.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Among the various approaches to computational linguistics, formal grammars are a link between linguistic theory and natural language processing (NLP). By formal grammars we mean fully explicit linguistic formalisms encoding the general principles and operations involved in generating syntactic structure. In contrast, the Penn-Treebank (PTB; [4], [5]) and the Universal Dependencies [6] do not explicitly encode why something should be labeled in a certain way, and we therefore consider them labeling conventions rather than fully-fledged theories of syntax. It is hard to ensure that a labeling convention for complex structure is followed consistently. Formal grammars, on the other hand, not only encode complex linguistic hypotheses explicitly but, when implemented on the computer, also map sentences to structures automatically and are fully consistent. Any error in them can be fixed systematically, and any previously labeled data can then be re-labeled automatically.

Grammars take a long time to develop, and the structures they produce are harder to use than the annotation schemes developed specifically for NLP: parsing can be much slower, for example, and the software stack generally needs to be more complex. However, grammars remain one of the few clear and long-term links between linguistics and NLP. In recent practice, formal implemented grammars have been used for computer assisted language learning (CALL) applications, including grammar coaching [7,8,9]. They have also been used to create high quality treebanks to train semantic parsers [11,12,13]. In this paper, we present the latest version of a grammar which can be used to create such high quality training data for Spanish.

The Spanish Resource Grammar [16,17] is the second biggest implemented HPSG grammar (see § 2.1). With this new interface, the grammar can be used with the state-of-the-art HPSG parsers and tailored as necessary. The work we present is unusual in that we are breathing new life into a valuable resource which had remained dormant for at least 10 years. The paper is organized as follows.
